claim: Did you know… women who eat breakfast cereal are more likely to have boys?

studies.cite: Mathews et al. (2008), Proceedings of the Royal Society B
studies.finding: In 740 British women, 56% in the highest preconception energy-intake third had boys versus about 45% in the lowest third.
studies.verdict: A published, peer-reviewed analysis, later disputed on statistical grounds.

studies.cite: Young et al. (2009), Proceedings of the Royal Society B
studies.finding: Critique argued that the original tested 132 foods in two periods and that the cereal result is a multiple-testing false positive.
studies.verdict: Reanalysis: about 13 chance hits expected among 264 tests.

claim: Did you know… sugar makes children hyperactive?

studies.finding: A meta-analysis of 16 double-blind, placebo-controlled trials found no effect of sugar on children's behaviour or cognition.
studies.verdict: Pooled trials show no measurable effect of sugar on behaviour.

studies.cite: Hoover & Milich (1994), Journal of Abnormal Child Psychology
studies.finding: Mothers told their sons had been given sugar rated them more hyperactive, although every boy had received a sugar-free placebo.
studies.verdict: Parental expectation, not sugar, shaped what they saw.

claim: Did you know… vitamin D pills prevent cancer and heart disease in healthy adults?

studies.cite: Manson et al. (2019), New England Journal of Medicine
studies.finding: In 25,871 adults followed 5.3 years, vitamin D3 at 2,000 IU daily did not lower invasive cancer or major cardiovascular events.
studies.verdict: Hazard ratios near 1 (0.96 and 0.97) for both primary endpoints.

claim: Did you know… eating too little salt is linked to more heart attacks and deaths?

studies.cite: O'Donnell et al. (2014), New England Journal of Medicine
studies.finding: In 101,945 people in 17 countries, both very high and very low estimated sodium intake were associated with more deaths and cardiovascular events.
studies.verdict: Observational J-shaped curve; estimates from single urine samples remain contested.

studies.cite: Sacks et al. (2001), New England Journal of Medicine
studies.finding: In 412 people eating each of three sodium levels for 30 days, lower sodium steadily lowered blood pressure.
studies.verdict: Trial supports lowering salt for blood pressure; heart outcomes not tested.

claim: Did you know… fish oil capsules prevent heart attacks?

studies.finding: In 11,324 recent heart attack survivors, 1 gram daily of n-3 fatty acids cut death, heart attack and stroke by about 10 to 20%.
studies.verdict: Positive result in survivors of a recent heart attack.

studies.cite: ASCEND Study Collaborative Group (2018), New England Journal of Medicine
studies.finding: In 15,480 people with diabetes, fish oil capsules did not reduce serious vascular events versus olive oil over 7.4 years.
studies.verdict: Null in people with diabetes and no prior vascular disease.

claim: Did you know… processed meat is in the same cancer category as cigarettes?

studies.cite: IARC Monograph Working Group (2015), Lancet Oncology
studies.finding: A working group classed processed meat as carcinogenic and red meat as probably carcinogenic to humans.
studies.verdict: Same category means equally certain, not equally dangerous.

studies.cite: Johnston et al. (2019), Annals of Internal Medicine
studies.finding: A guideline panel suggested adults continue current red and processed meat intake, calling the evidence low-certainty and the advice weak.
studies.verdict: Contested: low-certainty evidence behind a weak recommendation.
